items.description: Here, author Karen Millie-James considers her Irish roots and Ireland’s history. She looks at the background to the Irish Troubles and what happened during the Troubles. items.title: Shadows, war, and finding Moomin joy
items.author: NPR (podcasts@npr.org)
items.description: The Moomins have been a beloved children’s series around the world for decades. And now these bright, whimsical, and colorful Finnish characters are starting to gain steam in America. Today on Throughline, the story of their creator and the tragic circumstances that gave them life. Guests: Boel Westin, professor emerita of literature at Stockholm University, and author of Tove Jansson: Life, Art, Words Stina Ekblad, actor (as the voice of Tove Jansson) Support public media with NPR+ and enjoy p…

items.title: The Avignon Papacy and the Fight for France: Part 5 - The Beginning of the End
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: The Avignon Papacy (1309-1376) was the period during which seven successive popes resided at Avignon, in modern-day southern France, rather than at Rome. It followed a bitter conflict between the papacy and King Philip IV of France, and the death of Pope Boniface VIII in 1303 marked a decisive shift in the balance of power within the Church. Talia Bega explains — and looks at where it was the beginning of the end for France. You can read part 1 on the Church in the 13th century here , part 2 on…

items.title: 1066: The Norman Conquest and the Birth of Medieval England: Stamford Bridge: The Battle That Changed 1066 – Part 3
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: By September 1066, England had become the prize in one of the most extraordinary succession crises of the medieval world. King Edward the Confessor was dead, Harold Godwinson occupied the English throne, and two powerful foreign rulers had already claimed that the crown belonged to them. Duke William of Normandy was preparing an invasion across the Channel, but before William could strike, another claimant had arrived in England. From Scandinavia came Harald Hardrada, King of Norway, one of the…

items.title: The Winchester Mystery House: A Factual Timeline of America's Most Famous Haunted Mansion Legend
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: Interest in historical sites where popular legend has substantially diverged from the documentary record has remained strong among readers of American history, particularly cases involving a private individual's life story overtaken by commercially convenient folklore after their death. The Winchester Mystery House in San Jose, California, represents one of the clearest such cases in American architectural and cultural history, and tracing its documentary record from beginning to end reveals a…

items.title: Alexander Cartwright: The Invention of Baseball’s Inventor
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: From Manhattan firehouses to Honolulu, the surprising life of the man history turned into baseball’s founding father. Brian D’Ambrosio explains. Said to be the New York Knickerbockers Base Ball Club, circa 1847 - Alexander Cartwright, top-centre. Source: Public domain, 19cbaseball.com , available here . items.title: Andrew Carnegie: Philanthropic Hero or Exploitative ‘Robber Baron’?
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: As one of the wealthiest figures in American history, Andrew Carnegie left behind a legacy that remains deeply contested among historians and the public alike. While his name is permanently memorialized on thousands of public libraries, universities, and cultural institutions across the globe, his rise to unprecedented economic dominance was achieved through methods that raise fundamental questions regarding the true human cost of his late-in-life generosity. Shubh Samant explains. A depiction…

items.title: The Forgotten Women Who Brought the Nazis to Justice
items.author: Sara Beth Haring
items.description: by Natalie Livingstone Glancing at Dame Laura Knight’s painting of the Nuremberg Trials below, you might assume the historic pursuit of Nazi war criminals was a strictly male affair. However, as author Natalie Livingstone reveals, that depiction is far from the whole truth. Sparked by her personal connection as the granddaughter of Holocaust survivors, in Read More » The post The Forgotten Women Who Brought the Nazis to Justice appeared first on The History Reader .

items.author: NPR (podcasts@npr.org)
items.description: Looksmaxxing, weight loss, and muscle building have fueled a massive craze for injectable peptides. Some natural and some synthetic. These injectables have unleashed a multi-billion-dollar gray-market industry online and a high-stakes frontier for the pharmaceutical industry. Today, we reach back to the quest to manufacture the first peptide-based medicine: Insulin. Guests: Alison Li, historian of science and medicine, author of J. B. items.title: The Tariff of 1828, Sectional Economics, and the Origins of States’ Rights Doctrine
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: The controversy surrounding the Tariff of 1828, often identified as the “Tariff of Abominations,” represents one of the earliest and clearest moments when sectional identity and constitutional theory collided in the early United States. What began as a dispute over duties on imported goods evolved into a foundational argument about the nature of the Union itself—an argument later carried forward by John C. Calhoun and ultimately echoed in the secession crisis of 1860–61. To understand why the t…

items.title: 1066: The Norman Conquest and the Birth of Medieval England: Three Kings and a Crown: The Road to Invasion – Part 2
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: When Edward the Confessor died on the 5th January 1066, England did not simply lose a king. It lost the political center around which a fragile succession had been organized. Within hours, the kingdom had a new ruler, but that ruler was immediately confronted by men who believed that the English crown belonged to them. Harold Godwinson had been crowned King of England, yet across the Channel Duke William of Normandy was preparing an invasion, while in Scandinavia Harald Hardrada, King of Norway…

items.title: Can the polygraph test really spot a lie?
items.author: NPR (podcasts@npr.org)
items.description: From dating shows to police interrogation rooms, the polygraph test has long been marketed as a way to detect deception. But can it really? And who decided we needed a truth machine in the first place? In this episode, a Throughline listener sends us on a quest to uncover the story of the lie detector. Guests: Ken Alder, professor of history at Northwestern University and author of The Lie Detectors: The History of an American Obsession Support public media with NPR+ and enjoy perks for over 25…

items.title: Carl von Clausewitz and Military Strategy: On War
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: Carl von Clausewitz is one of the most celebrated, referenced, and original military strategists: his magnum opus On War is eclipsed in popularity and impact on the philosophy of war only by The Art of War. The philosophy of war according to Clausewitz is illustrated in the book’s most enduring quote: ‘War is merely the continuation of politics by other means.’ Craig Heslop explains. Carl von Clausewitz by William Wach. Source: Public domain, available here. Meant For War Clausewitz began his r…

items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: As young men, both Winston Churchill and Napoleon’s only son were certain that destiny had marked them out for greatness. Here, Bilal Junejo asks why one lived to save his country while the other died at 21, remembered today as little more than a footnote. Winston Churchill in 1900. items.title: Is the death penalty cruel and unusual?
items.author: NPR (podcasts@npr.org)
items.description: The Eighth Amendment. What is cruel and unusual punishment? Who gets to define and decide the amendment's boundaries? And how did the Constitution's authors imagine it might change? In this hour, the shifting definition of cruel and unusual punishment. This episode was originally published in January 2025. Guests: John Bessler , law professor at the University of Baltimore School of Law, and adjunct professor at the Georgetown University Law Center. Author of The Death Penalty's Denial of Funda…

items.title: A Heroic Bond in World War Two: After Operation Jubilee
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: A casual chat between two neighbours in snow-covered Edgemont, Alberta, Canada, led to an unexpected connection between two sons—one from the freezing Canadian winter and the other from a bushfire-ravaged property in Queensland, Australia. Their fathers shared a heroic bond during World War Two, and neither family knew of the other’s existence before their contact. Ken Wright and Anne Gafiuk explain. items.title: Dead Mountain: The Dyatlov Pass Incident and the Cold War Secrecy That Kept It a Mystery
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: On the night of February 1, 1959, nine experienced hikers pitched a tent on the open eastern shoulder of Kholat Syakhl, a bare, wind-scoured mountain in the northern Urals whose Mansi name is usually translated as "Dead Mountain." Sometime that night they cut their way out of the tent and walked, most of them without boots, toward a forest a mile away. None of them came back. For sixty years the deaths of the Dyatlov group were treated as one of the great unsolved puzzles of the twentieth centu…

items.author: Sara Beth Haring
items.description: by Connor Williams What can Americans learn about our divided country today from the Civil War that divided us in the past? items.title: Why does everything get a standing ovation now?
items.author: NPR (podcasts@npr.org)
items.description: Call it standing ovation inflation: these days, it feels like it's mandatory to stand and clap for live performances. Has our please clap era gone too far? That's what one Throughline listener wanted to know. So we traced the winding road from Shakespeare’s epilogues to Broadway divas to ridiculously long film festival ovations… and how they helped engineer the way we applaud. Guests: Roger Gilbert, professor in the Department of Literatures in English at Cornell Kyle Buchanan, reporter and col…

items.title: 1066: The Norman Conquest and the Birth of Medieval England: England Before the Storm: The World of 1066 – Part 1
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: In the year 1066, England stood at the edge of one of the most consequential transformations in its history. It was not an impoverished or primitive kingdom waiting to be rescued by a more advanced civilization. On the contrary, England was wealthy, organized and politically sophisticated, with an established legal system, an effective administration, a powerful Church and a highly developed network of towns and markets. Yet within a single year, the kingdom would be invaded from abroad, its ki…

items.title: The Last Celtic Voice in Anatolia: What a Sixth-Century Monk Tells Us About the Ancient Galatian Language
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: Languages disappear twice. First, people stop speaking them. Later, the archive makes the disappearance look cleaner than it ever was. A language used in homes, markets, jokes, arguments, and work can leave almost no literature if another language controls government, schooling, religion, and durable writing. Ancient Galatian is a brutal example. Celtic-speaking migrants reached central Anatolia in modern-day Turkey in the 3rd century BCE, built political communities there, and then lived for c…

items.title: Remembering Lillian Smith
items.author: Sara Beth Haring
items.description: by Keri Leigh Merritt Lillian Smith was a remarkable Southern white woman who fought to end segregation as early as the 1930s. She wrote multiple bestselling books which were censored, banned, and burned across the country. Unfortunately, many people have no idea who she is today. In the piece below, An Inconvenient Woman author and Read More » The post Remembering Lillian Smith appeared first on The History Reader .

items.title: Russia Since 1991: A Change for the Better?
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: This December will mark for the people of Russia one of the most defining moments in their history; the 35th anniversary of the dissolution of the Soviet Union. A major world power that had existed for nearly 70 years , its collapse reflected other significant developments in Eastern Europe at that time, where long-established communist regimes fell one by one and national boundaries changed dramatically, with Yugoslavia similarly dissolving, Czechoslovakia splitting into the two separate natio…

items.title: Four Seasons of Ceasefire in Gaza
items.author: NPR (podcasts@npr.org)
items.description: NPR’s Anas Baba is one of the last remaining journalists in Gaza working full-time for an American news organization. A year into the ceasefire, more than 1400 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, nearly 5,000 injured. And those numbers rise nearly every day. What has the last year looked and felt like on the ground? In this episode, Baba takes us through four seasons of ceasefire—as both a resident trying to survive and a reporter trying to document reality. Guests: Anas Baba, NPR Gaza…

items.title: Hilletie van Olinda: The Mohawk-Dutch Interpreter and Indigenous American Frontierswoman Who Played a Pivotal Role in the Fate of Empires
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: In an age when women were seldom recognized for their accomplishments, Hilletie van Olinda, a biracial Mohawk-Dutch woman who rose to become the official interpreter of the English Crown in the 1690s, received ample praise from both prominent Native American chieftains and the leading Euro-American government officials of her day. And yet, few people today know that a working Indigenous American woman played a pivotal role in the fate of empires during King William’s War, fought between England…

items.title: Charles Hatfield: The Man Who Made It Rain Too Well
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: In the winter of 1916, a city that had begged the sky for mercy got exactly what it asked for, and then some. Within weeks, dams had burst, bridges had vanished, and an estimated twenty people were dead. Standing at the center of it all was a former sewing machine salesman who had promised San Diego rain and delivered a flood. His name was Charles Hatfield. History would settle on a simpler title: the Rainmaker. Ansar Ali explains. Charles Hatfield in 1922. Source: Public domain, Farmers Almana…

items.title: Featured Excerpt: The Phantom
items.author: Sara Beth Haring
items.description: by Bob Drury and Tom Clavin Germans knew U.S. Marine Pete Ortiz as Das Fantom. They had placed a half a million French francs on his head because of his work in Nazi-occupied Europe as a scout, spy, saboteur, and French Resistance leader. In The Phantom, authors Bob Drury and Tom Clavin reveal the untold Read More » The post Featured Excerpt: The Phantom appeared first on The History Reader .

items.title: King John: The Fall and Death of King John - Part 6
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: To conclude the series on King John and the Magna Carta it is vital to review the whole, due to the extensive consequences that a short period in history had upon the future. Therefore, by, the autumn of 1216, King John's reign had become a desperate struggle for survival. The monarch who had once ruled an immense Angevin empire now faced rebellion within England, invasion from France, and the collapse of the authority he had spent years trying to preserve. items.title: Famous Toymaker, Olympian and so much more: A.C. Gilbert
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: The Erector Set construction toy has given joy to boys and girls throughout its existence in America. However, not many people know the man behind the creation of the Erector Set, A.C. Gilbert. He had an active and playful life in his youth. He achieved considerable success in athletics. His creation of the Erector Set was his greatest achievement. He was also credited with “saving Christmas” during World War I. Alfred Carlton Gilbert left a lasting mark on the fields of athletics, entertainmen…

items.title: The Painter and the Dictator: Vincent van Gogh, Adolf Hitler and the War on Modern Art
items.author: History Is Now Magazine
items.description: The lives of Vincent van Gogh and Adolf Hitler are rarely considered together. Here, Nethmi Samaranayaka looks at two men who both hoped to make their way as artists, and at how the regime one of them led would later seize the paintings of the other. items.description: We live in a moment with almost daily reminders of how fragile life on Earth is whether it be from climate change, nuclear weapons or AI. In this episode, we bring you a story from the not-so-distant past when we learned what drove dinosaurs to extinction. And how it might have helped us avoid the same end.
